utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. No preliminaries. Therefore, could the witness be escorted in the courtroom. Meanwhile, I address the following matter. That is about 92 bis statement. On the 8, the 10th and 17th of September of this year, the Chamber conditionally admitted Rule 92 bis packages for Zeljka Milinovic, Draga Milinovic, Bozo Davidovic, respectively. In those decisions six-week deadlines were imposed for filing relevant attestations and declarations. The Chamber notes that these have not been filed nor has the Chamber received any communication from the Defence regarding these deadlines. The Chamber reminds the Defence that the Zeljka Milinovic's, Draga Milinovic's, and Bozo Davidovic's evidence will not be admitted unless the declarations and attestations are submitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Marjanovic, I assume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we start, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Marjanovic. Mr. Marjanovic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You'll find Mr. Stojanovic to your left. Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Marjanovic.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to tell us your name and surname, which is what we usually do here in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Ostoja Marjanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, could you please tell me when you were born and where.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in 1942 in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like that to ask you to describe your schooling and professional career to us in brief terms.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I graduated from high school. After that I got a degree from the University of Belgrade in mining. In the 1970s, I started working in the Ljubija iron-ore mines. In professional terms, I first worked as head of shift and then worked my way up to general manager and that is the post I assumed on the 1st of October [as interpreted], 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court -- did I understand you correctly: The 1st of February, 1991? Until when were you general manager of the Ljubija mines?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: From the 1st of February, 1991, I was president of the management board as it was called in those days and that's what I was until the end of 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just for the transcript, it seems to me that on page 3, line 3, it says the 1st of October, 1991, and the witness actually said the 1st of February, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. To the extent there was an error in the transcription it has been rectified, it has been corrected by your follow-up question and the answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court, Mr. Marjanovic, whether you did your regular military service and whether you had any kind of military training.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1969, I did my military service, one year in the air force, and I was just a foot soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After serving in the military doing your regular military service, did you have any kind of rank in the military?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, in November, as a volunteer, I joined the air force of Republika Srpska, and I was given the rank of second lieutenant because I was a sports pilot.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After the multi-party elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina, were you politically involved at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Towards the end of 1993 and then up until August 1994, I was vice-president of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, and since, at that time the Serbian Democratic Party, the SDS, appointed personnel, at that moment I was a member of that party, therefore, but when I resigned in August 1994, I left the party as well. Sorry, may I just add one more thing. After the Dayton Accords in 1996, I was a member of the democratic party from Serbia. I was in the Main Board. I was on the Main Board. It was Mr. Djindjic's party. I supposed to organise the party in Bosnia in Republika Srpska. Because our programme concept for Republika Srpska differed, I -- we therefore parted ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you said that from 1991 to 1996, you were president of the management board of the Ljubija mine, I would like that ask you to explain to us a bit here in the courtroom what that means and what these duties are. What is it that the president of the management board of a mine does?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you allow me, I'm going to give you the organisational chart of the Ljubija mines in the briefest possible terms and you will understand my duties on that basis. The mine consisted of 24 organisational units. Three of them were production based. That, the central, eastern -- central mine, Eastern Mines or Tomasica and Omarska, and then all of these units were headed by directors. I chaired this management board that these directors were members of and they had their offices where the mines were and I was in the city of Prijedor so, according to the statute, as the general manager, I acted on the basis of the law and my relations with the state were based on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, until 1992, how many employees were there in the Ljubija mines?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: When I assumed my post on the 1st of February, 1991, the total number of employees was 4.730. It was a mixed ethnic group in Ljubija, there were Czechs and Poles and Ukrainians, who practically stayed there after the first world war and that's where they worked. And already in 1916, when Austro-Hungary started production in those mines, they started living and working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As the war developed did the number of employees go down and did the ethnic composition of the employees of the mine become any different?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: After what happened in May 1992, and then throughout 1992, the structure changed. All of these unfortunate events -- well, I have to mention that part of the employees who were ethnic Croats and Muslims left Prijedor already at the end of 1991. However, all these other unfortunate events that took place in April, May, June 1992 made people leave Prijedor so the structure changed significantly, especially the mine. It was not operating. So I could not actually see what the ethnic composition was like. Also, quite a few of the employees from the Ljubija mines were involved in the brigades, the 43rd Brigade and the 5th Kozara Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As management, as the manager of the mine, did you ever pursue a policy of discrimination against employees who were non-Serbs in terms of their further employment?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Since the number of employees went down and the activity of the mine as well, I had the powers to impose work obligation. I testified here earlier on and I had documents that showed orders on work obligation and the structure was heterogenous.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Until when was the mine operating and until when was it delivering ore?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, it wasn't 1991. 1992. In the beginning of March, it delivered iron-ore to the Zenica steel mill and after all of these well-known events, production stopped everywhere, and even equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just interrupt, Mr. Stojanovic. Sir, you were asked whether you did ever pursue a policy of discrimination against employees who were non-Serbs in terms of their further employment. I don't think I understood your answer. Did you or did you not practice that policy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise to you. Since I said that on the basis of my orders on work obligation, that is to say, I -- I thought that I had responded when I said that the people who had work obligation this different ethnic backgrounds. So, no, I did not pursue any kind of policy of discrimination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, in view of what it was that we called you here for, I would like to draw your attention to some questions that would be - how do I put this? - significant for us here. The company that you headed, did it, in 1992, have any kind of construction mechanization in the sense of bulldozers, excavators and other heavy construction machinery?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: You've already responded by putting this question. It is hydraulic excavators and electric bulldozers, Caterpillars, Russian-made, 789, those are the types, that is. So we had several such pieces of equipment but this was mining equipment for mines. That is to say -- but we also had construction equipment for construction as such, for constructing buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber the following: When you say that part of the mine included the eastern mine, what do you mean by this, eastern mine, or what did you mean in the company itself when you say that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's implied because it's 18 kilometres to the east of Prijedor. The place where the pits are are Busnovi and Maric village. I don't know where the name Tomasica comes from and which period it dates back to because the villages are named, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But to make things clearer, this name, Tomasica, does it correspond to that concept in the economic and business sense of your company, which is Eastern Mines?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In our business documents, you will also find the name Eastern Mines, as well as Tomasica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of works were carried out there until 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a classical open-pit mine. The ore was lying at a depth of 150 metres and the width of the pit was 20 to 30. First of all, the useless layers are removed to reveal the ore. The ore is transported by dumpers to Susari, I'm talking about the Eastern Mines, where it is voided of about 20, 30 per cent of moisture and the product thereof is transported to Smederovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This kind of works, were they carried out at Eastern Mines or Tomasica until February 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, all the three units of production in the manufacturing of ore were active.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did it imply the need for heavy machinery to be used in Eastern Mines, some of the machinery that the Ljubija mines had until 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of February and beginning of March, through the managers of production units, I ordered that all the heavy machinery, those are machines over 50 tonnes each, be placed in maintenance garages where it was maintained and serviced so that the engines be repaired and the oil stirred so that certain assemblies would not be removed or taken away. That means that the heavy machinery used in Eastern Mines and Omarska was in mechanical shops, and a certain number of people were taking care of the maintenance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: With the outbreak of war in Croatia in 1991 and in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992, did there occur a requisitioning of this equipment and machinery belonging to the company which you headed at the time?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, already in 1991. A smaller part of our equipment was requisitioned, mainly bulldozers, for the needs of the 43rd Brigade, mainly. And these requisitioning lists still exist, I believe, in the old part of the mine. One part of the Ljubija mine is now ArcelorMittal company. I believe the owners are in London.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you tell the Court briefly how does this requisitioning process go legally and in practice?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The representative of a military unit either comes personally or sends something in writing to present their demand for certain machines. They fill out forms to confirm that they requisitioned a certain machine. In the requisitioning paper, although they sometimes ask for operators to be supplied too - I did not do that because I didn't have the right to send men together with the machines - and then they would take the machine away and transport them -- haul them away, basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: From the moment a machine is requisitioned, who manages the machine, who makes requests for its use and who is responsible for it?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's exclusively the entity that requisitioned it. I have to stress here that sometimes it happened that I would get information from my personnel that a certain machine -- attempts are made to -- to take away a certain machine. And then I had to intervene for the machine to remain the property of the Ljubija mine, despite the fact that it's being used by a particular military unit. If you allow me, I'll give you an example. In 1994, a drill of 230 millimetres diameter was used in building the road from Laniste to Banja Luka. A civil engineering from Laktasi was using it for these works and when I got information that they were trying to take this drill away permanently, then I asked the owner of that company or the manager of that company to warehouse this drill in our own depot and the head of that company took that drill back to Ljubija, where I believe it still is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did it happen ever that a machine requisitioned by the JNA or later the VRS remain in the mine, or was it taken away for the purposes of some military task?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was mainly transported to another area where it was used in works. My assumption, if I may say it, was that the army used bulldozers to build roads in impassable areas where they were active.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the question was whether it happened that the machinery stayed in the mine. Now you said it mainly was transported to another area, but the question was: Did it happen that the machinery was not transported to another area but remained in the mine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of my knowledge, every machine that was requisitioned was transported away from the mine and returned when the works were finished. I will give you the example of Koricanske Stijene where the Security Services Centre from Prijedor requisitioned part of our equipment and five days later returned it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And upon return, was it on -- formally handed over again to the mine or -- so that the mine would be responsible for the equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, the management of the mine, and you, as the director, have the possibility to oppose requisitioning of your equipment that was the property of the mine?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. There was no such possibility. We could not prohibit the requisitioning of either people or equipment. That is to say, we could not oppose mobilisation or requisitioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the legislations prevailing in 1991, was it at all possible to oppose any requisitioning of machines when they were required for the defence of the country?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not very familiar with the legislation, but I'm sure it was not possible to oppose it because, in the beginning of 1991, it was in the interests of the state to engage all the resources for defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you something else now, related to the organisation of the operation of the mine. At that time, in 1991, 1992 and the other years of war, did your mine have active security around the whole complex and inside it?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: As part of the mine complex, there are two dams for sludge disposal in Ljubija and in Omarska. In the end of 1991 and beginning of 1992, there was a units of popular defence within the mine, and they had some weapons. Upon my orders, the weapons were given to local communities to defend the dams from demolition or collapse. The flood, any flood resulting from the collapse of a dam would destroy all the settlements downstream. Until May 1992, this worked well. After that, the whole amount of the equipment was returned to the mine and upon my orders again, all this equipment was given to the military unit in Palanciste, together with the explosives that were used in the mining. I cannot be very precise about whether this was exactly in May or in April but in any case all of the weapons and part of the -- part of the uniforms were given to the military unit I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sir, what are units of popular defence? Were these security guards employed by the mine or were these members of the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had this doctrine of All People's Defence, which means the army and the people together. That doctrine prevailed in the former Yugoslavia and it implied that, in the case of the danger of war, all of us had the obligation to be mobilised and accordingly we were issued uniforms and everything except weapons. We also got certain sets of equipment against chemical weapons et cetera. So most of the military-age men had equipment and had uniforms and that's the kind of unit I'm talking about. As opposed to the security detail of the mine which, according to the law, had different uniforms and short-barrelled weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And did I understand you correctly that you earlier did say these units of popular defence did have weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one follow-up question. You earlier said that ... that: "Weapons were given to local communities to defend the dams ..." What local communities are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope to make this clear. These weapons were stored in the depot of the mine, and local communes are Ljubija, Omarska and Tomasica. Especially Ljubija and then Omarska. Exclusively for the purpose of these dams where sludge was deposited into such a large embankment as to form a dam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it's still not clear. Through what channels were the local communes provided with weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A certain amount of weapons that were stored in the mine were directly issued to the president of the local commune. I remember in Ljubija it was a Muslim woman who was the president of the local commune, and they kept guard duty at these dams to prevent sabotage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What quantity should I think of? For example, the Ljubija, how many weapons did you give to the president of the local commune, that Muslim woman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If my memory serves me well, not more than six automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At any point in time after 1992, did the Army of Republika Srpska physically secure the mine?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The people who were the security detail of the mine, during the war years, did they wear a uniform?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I've said before that there was a special unit of security men who wore a distinctive uniform. Each mine had its distinctive uniform, and they had small-arms. In the beginning of 1992, anybody could wear a uniform for several reasons. First of all, we all had one. The so-called SNB uniform, the olive-green grey. And, second, that somehow elevated the person wearing the uniform. And, third, it was a kind of protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were these men serving their work obligation in the mine or were they members of a military unit?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can say this. Some workers who were doing their work obligation wore that uniform, but the uniform was also worn by civilians and others inside the villages. It was difficult at that time to say why somebody is wearing a uniform. I repeat: Almost everybody was wearing a uniform. There was even an order in May 1992 that all managers of companies had to wear a uniform, and I had to wear one too sometime until the end of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... was this uniform the same as the uniform worn by the soldiers, by the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the first stage, it was mostly military uniforms of the former JNA. In the later stage, they varied. There were camouflage uniforms, there were those that just involved a jacket. Then there were SNB ones, olive-green-grey. All sorts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But did they belong to the military, to the VRS, now that the JNA was no longer there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how to answer. I cannot say either yes or no. I've just explained that most citizens wore uniforms. They didn't belong to the defence or the army at all. They just wore uniforms for their own protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. But what I'm asking you is whether these uniforms that these people wore were they similar to those worn by the VRS or was it possible by looking at various units to say, That is an army uniform and that is not an army uniform. It's a uniform of something else that I may not know. Or was it indistinguishable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could not make a distinction --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ostoja. What about the Eastern Mines, or Tomasica as we've been calling it? At that time, in 1992 onward, did it also have its own security, physical security that we've been speaking of until now?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, as for industrial facilities, in this area that we call area that we called Tomasica, what was there within that complex?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The road that leads to the facilities actually leads to a gate so that civilians could not enter. After the gate, there is the management building with a restaurant. Then further on, there is a service shop to the right. Then, on the left is the so-called sitara. That is actually a plant where the mine -- where the ore is further dealt on. Further on from the sitara, there is a plant for drying ore in two furnaces. Then, further on, there is a mixing plant where the ore is brought in and undergoes this process. There was another gate too, in addition to the one that I spoke of. It's about 100 metres away and it entered the compound of Ferox. That is a plant that was built on the basis of natural pigment. They had a mini-plant, a drying plant, a mixing plant, and they were a integral whole. That is to say, they were an independent entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please have in e-court an aerial image. It is 32665. That's its 65 ter number. So that all of this would be a bit clearer to us, everything that the witness spoke of. 65 ter 32665.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I, meanwhile, ask a follow-up question to the witness. You said there was an order sometimes that managers had to wear uniforms as well and you did now and then as well. Who gave that order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do you remember when that order was given.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said in May, and I remember that I wore a uniform, say, up until the end of June. I could not give you the precise date. 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, at the moment of issuing that order, was it still multi-ethnically composed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you please take a look at the screen in front of you? You will see a photograph. And I'd like to ask you the following: Can you recognise this area depicted in the aerial image?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Trial Chamber specifically what area this is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please speak into the microphone and could other microphones please be switched off. We cannot understand him at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you're invited - and perhaps the microphone could be slightly adjusted as well - to speak into the microphone so that your words will not be lost. And perhaps you repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the road that leads to the Eastern Mines from the direction of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could I just stop you at this point and I'm going to ask our usher for assistance. If you could use the pen to draw an arrow in the form of an arrow to mark the direction leading to the mine of Tomasica.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the direction leading from Prijedor to Tomasica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The road to Maricka goes to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please don't hold this against me, but I'm going to ask you step by step. In order to make clearer for us could you mark on this map using a line, can you mark the barrier that was the check-point that allowed access to this entire area, the area called Tomasica.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The initially built one was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark that with the letter A.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: A. The second is in this area here. That's B. That is the access route to Ferox.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark the first access point again. We said we would mark it with the letter A.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's it. And this is the letter A.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you put the letter A there?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness has done that, Mr. Stojanovic. We see a letter A is the upper one in the right lower-hand corner, just above where the witness made a B. And immediately left from the A and the B, he marked the entrances, the gates. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you put a circle around the facilities that are on the left-hand side immediately after the first access point; and could you please tell the Trial Chamber what are these buildings in relation to the ones that you mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about gate B. This here is the Ferox plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please put the letter F there.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The letter F.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Above, we also see some buildings. Could you please put a circle around them and could you tell what you say kind of buildings these are, what kind of facilities these are?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: When one enters through gate A, to the right is the management building with the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please put UZ there, [B/C/S spoken]?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Then is the service shop, PSR, [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to tell us what kind of facility this is, the one above the PSR to the left of this road?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you allow me, I would like to draw your attention to the following. To the left of the PSR is the sitara. That is where the ore is processed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: As the road goes on, there's the drying plant, where the ore is dried.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Further on?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The road continues to the open pit of the Eastern Mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1992, 1993, 1994 and 1995, these four years of war, who provided physical security for all these facilities at these two points?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: People from the Ljubija mines provided security for the PSR and the facilities for preparing ore. People from Ferox, that's a special department not within the mine, they provided security for these facilities of Ferox.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Members of the Army of Republika Srpska, did they provide physical security at any point in time at these two points that you marked just now?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not at all. To the best of my knowledge, and I had to receive information these directors there who covered certain facilities. At the end of 1995, all the way up until the end of 1995, the military did not provide security for any part of these mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The mentioned persons who provided this physical security, did they have any kind of military weapons or any kind of personal weapons for that matter, if not military?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: As for guards from Ljubija, I already mentioned that they had short-barrelled weapons. As for the people from Ferox, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, do you want to tender this marked aerial view of the area?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Just one more question which would involve the necessity of further marking perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, just in order to make things clearer for us as we went through this yesterday, this -- this body of water, this lake, if I may call it that, could you please tell us what this is about or, rather, the two lakes that we see in this photograph? What are they?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The first lake above these plants is the lake of the open pit. This dates back to 1988 because water came through and then the exploitation of the mine stopped. To the north is a deposit of waste and that is how this second lake was created.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this aerial image be admitted into evidence. It is 65 ter now 32665.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we proceed to that, I'd like to clarify that where the witness said the road continues to the open pit of the Eastern Mines, that is when he added some arrow-shaped markings going from what he marked as S first to the right and then later further up. No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour. Just for the record, I understood Mr. Stojanovic to be tendering the exhibit as marked by the witness, but it wasn't clear from the words he used. So I just wanted to make sure I understood what I wasn't objecting to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I earlier asked whether he wanted to have this tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, aerial view marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives Exhibit D1347, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1347 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a few more questions before the break, Mr. Witness. Tell us, during 1992, 1993, 1994, 1995, in this area of the Eastern Mines called Tomasica was there any construction machinery that had not been mobilised and that was nevertheless in this area?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you remember, could you please tell us what kind of machines these were or what kind of machine this was that had not been mobilised and that stayed in the area?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The completed equipment for the open pit was there. Dumpers, Caterpillar 70-tonnes bulldozers, Caterpillar graders, G 16. We call this -- we called this small-scale mechanization, that is to say, for maintenance, excavators that were used for selective excavation. I think that there were small buses there, up to 12 seats, for the transportation of workers while there was still exploitation. Practically, the entire mechanization that is indispensable for the operation of the open pit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's time for the break. You said you would have a few questions before the break but how many questions would you have at all for the witness? Because I think you scheduled him for one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. I think I have about ten questions left. And I think that within the next 15 minutes or so, I will complete the direct examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then first take the break and you'll have 15 minutes after the break. Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness to enter the courtroom, I briefly deal with the Defence filing of the -- of Rule 92 bis motions after the deadline set by the Chamber. On the 17th of August of this year, the Chamber set the deadline of 18th September for the Defence to file any remaining Rule 92 bis motions. This can be found at transcript page 37908. The Chamber notes that on 29 October, the Defence filed a Rule 92 bis motion in relation to Mile Matijevic with no explanation as to why the motion was being filed six weeks after the deadline. The Chamber would like to hear oral submissions from the Defence as to why this motion was filed late within the next 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can say now, Your Honour, that witness is in connection to Tomasica, so probably by that time we didn't have everything sorted out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but at least such an explanation should be provided if you file such a motion. Whether that is a valid reason I leave that open for the time being, but at least you should have paid attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there are any further submissions by either party, we'd like to hear tomorrow. Witness, we'll now continue. Mr. Stojanovic has another 15 minutes of questions for you. Please proceed. And the Chamber would appreciate, Mr. Stojanovic, that you put such questions that we can easily link them to what the core of the case is and what is the evidence is presented by the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, did there come a time during the war when the Army of Republika Srpska was physically present at the Eastern Mines of Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: There is one period, and I cannot tell you precisely which month but it was in 1994, when the 6th Sana Brigade, or a part of it, passed through Tomasica and spent the night there. Which unit and how large it was, I don't know. This is something that I was told by a soldier who travelled with me from Brcko to Prijedor and he told me that he had been in our laboratory where they broke some equipment and he was talking to me without knowing that I'm the manager of that mine, whereupon he got a bit scared. But that's the only time when army troops were at the Eastern Mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When in 1992 was the 43rd Prijedor Brigade there, mobilising people?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: That brigade was holding positions facing Gradacac, and the 5th Kozara Brigade was in the area of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did there come any time during the years of war when you had occasion to meet with General Mladic in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I never met the general in those four or five years. Although I had been invited when Karadzic or Krajisnik and others visited. To the best of my knowledge, Mr. Mladic has never been in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that also apply to 1993, 1994, and 1995?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. From the beginning of 1992 until the Dayton Accords, I never saw him at any meeting that I attended, nor did I hear from anyone else that he had been in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You, as manager of the mine, did you have any obligation to report or inform the Army of Republika Srpska, its Main Staff or the Command of the 1st Krajina Corps about the developments inside or around the Ljubija mines?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I had no such obligation. As for activities inside the mine, the keeping of the equipment and security and protection, I reported to the board of the municipality of Prijedor, in fact, the Secretariat for economy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As manager of the mine, did you have any knowledge about the burial of corpses around your area?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, none. When I appeared here as a witness in 2003, I was shown a map where these grave-sites were identified and then I saw that it was not only Tomasica but Jakarina Kosa and some others were grave-sites -- sites of mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When did you testify? In which case and when did you receive that information for the first time?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe it was 2003, the month of March. The case was Stakic. I spent four days in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time or perhaps later, did you have any knowledge from where these bodies were brought to be buried there?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no knowledge at all. Anything I could say would be an assumption, but I believe my assumptions do not matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And to conclude, do you personally have any knowledge about who led this process of gathering these bodies, the sanitization of the terrain and the burial of the bodies in these areas?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I may use an analogy, if the public security centre from Prijedor sanitized the terrain around Prijedor, Koricanske Stijene and knowing a little about the work of the public security centre and its responsibilities and independence, my guess is that it was done by the public security centre of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answers. Knowing about your health situation, we have no further questions at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Fluegge has a question before we give an opportunity to the Prosecution to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, a minute ago you were asked by

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: "When in 1992 was the 43rd Prijedor Brigade there, mobilising people?" I'm not sure if you have answered that question. It was recorded that you would have said that brigade was holding position facing Gradacac. Again, please answer the question: When in 1992 was the 43rd Prijedor Brigade there, mobilising people, if you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. Because the 43rd Brigade was in Slavonia. When they moved from Slavonia to the area of Gradacac, I don't know exactly, but it was in 1992. Because my men who were in that unit were returning home from that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Traldi. You'll find Mr. Traldi to your right. Mr. Traldi is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago that you testified in the Stakic case. You were also interviewed by staff of the Office of the Prosecutor in July of last year; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Is it your position that you told the truth on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I do. I do claim that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now from 1991 to 1996, and indeed since then, you lived in Prijedor town; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions about the company now. Before the war, RZR Ljubija was the largest employer in Prijedor municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It was a state-owned company?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a state-owned company.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you mentioned on direct examination, at temporary transcript page 4, that from 1993 to 1994 you were vice-president of the Municipal Assembly Executive Board. You hadn't been a member of the SDS before that but you joined the SDS to hold that position; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I joined the SDS because I accepted the position of vice-president of the Executive Board in order to be able to act within that party.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And Slobodan Balaban, one of the other officials at RZR Ljubija, he was a member of the SDS Municipal Board in Prijedor; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. He was not a member of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I think my speed of speech may have been off. Let me re-ask the question and make sure the translation is correct. Mr. Balaban, one of the other officials at RZR Ljubija, was a member of the SDS Municipal Board in Prijedor municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now when you served as vice-president on the Executive Board, the vice-president of the municipality was a man known as Cigo; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: He'd commanded a VRS unit in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think so. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 32093.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is part of the 4th Tactical Group bulletin from May of 1994. Looking at the first paragraph in the text below the heading, we see a reference to fighters from Mount Kozara setting off on what it describes as the Serb people's decisive battle for survival. And it refers to the fighters of the 2nd and 5th Battalions strengthened by the Cigo and Zolja strike groups. The Cigo group, that's the one commanded by the vice-president of the municipality at the time you served on the Executive Board, Momcilo Radanovic; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's the end of 1992, I suppose. At that time I think - but I cannot be sure - that he was vice-president in the Municipal Assembly from Autumn 1993 to August 1994 when I resigned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, if are you interested in a complete transcript, then you really should slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I take the point, Your Honour, and I am interested in a complete transcript. I'll tender the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 32093 receives exhibit number P7620, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7620 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 32859.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As it comes up you also served on the SDS commission for information and propaganda in 1994; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, you are invited to repeat the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, a number of a document which we thought would not have been released but has been released by now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we that document, please, 65 ter 32859.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now this is a decision on the election of members of the commission for information and propaganda. We see under members your name first and below you, Ostoja Kesar. Now, he was the editor of Kozarski Vjesnik and of Radio Prijedor; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 31040.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Anything you'd like to do with the present document, Mr. Traldi?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I will tender it. It's related to the next two and so I'd thought to do them together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You take them together. We'll wait for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is an undated list of SDS Municipal Board commissions. Under commission for information and propaganda, we see your name and Mr. Kesar's again. Then under political council at number 2, we see Slobodan Balaban. That's the RZR Ljubija official we discussed earlier; right.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: With your leave, I was a member of the commission, and there was only one meting held and no more. And Mr. Balaban was the director of clay trade company at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And can we have 65 ter 14313A. And we're looking for the top of the page in the B/C/S, the second point. And this is the programme orientation and editorial policy of Kozarski Vjesnik and Radio Prijedor. We see in the second point: "Both these information media, especially at this wartime, must act as a political platform of the Serb nation, Army of Republika Srpska, as well as of political and civilian government organs of the Serb nation." Now this was consistent with SDS policy; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I could not comment upon this. I was not part of the political leadership of the SDS and what is written here, I can't say anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You were part of the SDS information and propaganda committee as we saw a moment ago. You were the vice-president of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly, as you testified on direct examination. Are you sure you're unable to confirm whether what we see in front of us is consistent with the platform of an organisation for which you served on the propaganda and information commission?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you've been paying attention, I said only one meeting of the propaganda committee was held that I attended, and I never attended any more meetings, and the reason was that the concept that I advocated did not fit into the policies of the SDS. And for that reason, I cannot speak about or comment upon the programming orientation of this newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, in fact, sir, to be able to opine that your policy didn't fit in the SDS policy, you'd have to know what the SDS policy was; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: You are imputing that to me. I didn't have to know. I presented my views. The president of the committee did not agree with it. That was the only time when I was present there. And I never came again. The policies were created by the Main Board which also defined their tasks and charted policies. I was not part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What views did the president of the committee disagree with?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, the operation of the economy, the political leadership of the SDS replaced all heads of companies in Prijedor if they were not members of the SDS. My proposal was that it was the balance of the accounts of a company that should decide whether a manager should stay or go. Also, my view was that leaders of businesses should be decided by open contest. They did not agree with it. Instead, they said - and Karadzic confirmed it - that they had to be members of the SDS. Those were two of my proposals. They were both rejected, and there was no need even for any more debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm about to address that answer, Your Honours, but before I do, I tender the past three documents that's 32859 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives Exhibit P7621.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives Exhibit P7622.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And 14313A.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives Exhibit P7623.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you testified a moment ago about the SDS position on replacing heads of the companies. In fact, you know that the Prijedor Crisis Staff ordered that all the Muslims and Croats in all the companies be fired; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not receive that order from the Crisis Staff but from the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please answer the question. The question was whether you knew that the Crisis Staff ordered such dismissals. Not how you received it. The question is: Were you aware that this was ordered by the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was not aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 33385, page 235.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we look at that, but you did receive an order, although you say it reached you from the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is part of your OTP interview where you testified a moment ago you told the truth. You'd said the SDS did not trust you. The Crisis Staff did not trust you. "Because I was speaking," you say, "completely opposite than what they were speaking." And lower down on the page, you're asked: "What activities of the SDS Crisis Staff did you disagree with?" You answer: "With release of employees, for example." And turning to the next page, you were asked: "From the Ljubija mines company?" And you responded: "In all the companies. It was an order that employees, Muslims and Croats are to be fired, basically." Now, does that refresh your recollection as to your knowledge that the Prijedor Crisis Staff ordered Muslims and Croats in all the companies in Prijedor municipality to be fired?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that I received a proclamation by the Executive Board, specifically the Secretariat for the Economy, and I probably misspoke in this situation. I said I disagreed with the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going ask that a number be reserved for excerpts of the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, a number to be reserved for excerpts.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P7624, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll later see what you, and perhaps also the Defence, will upload from this interview and then we'll decide on whether or not to admit it as P7624.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Before I move on, sir, I'm going to ask Ms. Stewart to play the audio of 65 ter 33385a, another portion of your interview, also part of your discussion of what activities of the Crisis Staff you disagreed with that we saw on the previous page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, have transcripts been provided to the booth and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that, like with videos, in playing it a second round, we'll receive interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes. So we'll play it a second time now. And the booths received a transcript of his original words in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] After what happened in relation to the Crisis Staff, the cleansing of Prijedor, leveling the old town to the ground, there are quite a few things that they did, not to mention the establishment of the investigation centre that happened where my people were, and so on. I did not agree with that."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, in what way, when you said those words did you mean that Prijedor had been cleansed?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of May, an attack was carried out against Prijedor. There were three days of war operations. There was shelling and there were houses that were damaged. The Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor established a commission that was in charge of taking care of the effects of the shelling and the war operations. They mobilised equipment from the mine, and this equipment was involved in the cleaning of the debris from the buildings that were destroyed. It was at Berek that the heaviest fighting had been taking place, so that is practically where all the buildings were cleansed with mechanization. Although expropriation of that area had already taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now you mentioned in your recorded answer a place called Stari Grad. That's the old town of Prijedor, a Muslim neighbourhood; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I also mentioned that it was called Berek. It is one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the shelling you mentioned, that was done by the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know who it was. If I were to say anything, I would be making a mistake because I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You do know that -- you confirmed that a moment ago. You stand by, then, your words in the interview that we heard on the audio; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Stand by what? Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your words in the interview. The cleansing of Prijedor and the leveling of the old town to the ground. You stand by those things; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You mentioned there were three days of war operations. Now, while roundups of Muslims from the Stari Grad and other neighbourhoods continued, in fact, the VRS had control of the situation within a matter of hours; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned roundups of Muslims, I'm not aware of any such thing. I know that I spent three days in the house because these war operations were underway. They started about 4.00 a.m. on the 30th of May, and that went on for the next few days. I can say that at that time I was at home throughout, and I didn't dare go outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now these, the cleansing, the levelling, are these among the unfortunate events you referred to during direct examination that caused Muslims and Croats to leave Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that if you're linking this to the cleansing of the town, the old town, Berek that is, in that period there probably weren't any inhabitants there. The entire operation took place under the command of the commission that was established by the Executive Board. The assumption was since expropriation had taken place, the entire area had been expropriated, it is for that reason they were cleansing that area. There was supposed to be a sports centre there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Two follow-up questions. First, when you say in that period probably there weren't any inhabitants there, you mean the period when RZR Ljubija equipment was being used to knock down what remained of the buildings there; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, second, you mentioned the cleansing was something that you were opposed to in your interview. You wouldn't be opposed to the creation of a sports centre. What were you opposed to about the cleansing?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I have to draw your attention to something. That is the sports centre decision was taken a lot earlier, a year or two before that. An entire expropriation took place and quite a few of these people from Berek, from the old town, built beautiful houses in the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I understand you're focussing on the sports centre. I'd ask you to focus on the cleansing. What about the cleansing were you opposed to? What aspects of it.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Against destroying buildings that were in good condition and that were operational.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now we also heard in the recorded portion of your interview that we played a moment ago we heard you refer to an investigative centre. That was at one of the RZR Ljubija mines, Omarska; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. The first time I had a document containing instructions to establish an investigation centre was in 2003 when I testified. Simo Drljaca headed the public security centre and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm certainly not suggesting to you at the moment that you established the investigative centre, and I'll make very clear if I'm suggesting that you did. But I'd ask to you focus closely on the questions that I ask you so we can move through most efficiently. Now you did learn in late May 1992 that Omarska had been taken over; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't understand. I mean, we're not understanding each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sure. Did you learn in late May 1992 that the Omarska facility had been taken over by the army and the police.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. The police, yes. The army, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 33381, page 66.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is a part of the testimony in the Stakic case that you testified a moment ago was truthful. You're asked: "After the conflict in Kozarac, the facilities in Omarska -- your facilities in Omarska were taken and occupied. What can you tell us about the way this happened? " And you answered: "The director of Omarska was Dusko Vlacina. He was director of the production plant there. And the organisation of watching the facilities in Omarska was under his authority. I learned a few days after the incident in Kozarac that the army and the police had forcibly entered the facilities in Omarska." Now, do you stand by this portion of your Stakic testimony that I've just read back to you?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can confirm everything you said about that period except for the centre of public security. They practically entered the facility and they took up the management building and the work-shop. As for the army, that they entered, I cannot say that because they offered me a contact so that they could move into Omarska and I didn't want to sign that contract. But it's possible that they were there for a while. It's the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 33383, page 27. And as it comes up, I'll ask that an exhibit number be reserved for excerpts of the witness's Stakic testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps we already reserve that number now. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives exhibit number P7625, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the excerpts still to be determined finally, but this number is reserved. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now at the lower end of the page beginning at line 20, you were asked: "Sir, didn't you testify that you were aware of the mine being taken over by the army in May? Let me ask you: Weren't you aware in May that the army did what you described as a take-over of the Omarska mine?" And you answered: "That was the end of May." And then you gave a similar explanation. Turning to the next page, at the very bottom you were asked: "You told us that you became aware from security guards, I believe you told us -" and the lawyer says: "I'm looking for the page but I can't find it - that the army and police had entered the facility in late May. Is that correct? And you answer: "Correct." Do you stand by these two portions of your purportedly truthful Stakic testimony that I've just read back to you?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: It is possible, actually it is certain that the public security centre or, rather, part of the local population entered forcibly after having removed our guards and that they took the warehouses. I stand by that. They stole tools, equipment that they took to their own homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This -- Witness, you certainly are aware of what the gist of the question is. You carefully left out, apparently, whether the army was involved. You confirmed the police. It's now put to you that the three portions in your testimony that you said it was police and the army, and now in your answer to this question, you just -- you are silent on the army and pretend to have answered the question. You have not. Do you stand by your testimony in Stakic on these last two portions, as well as, as far as the army is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm 100 per cent sure about the public security centre. I'm not sure about the army, but it's possible. The JNA at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, I see you're eager to identify the army as the JNA. By the end of May in 1992, you know the army in Prijedor was the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I used the word "investigative centre" when I was -- when we introduced Omarska because it was what you'd said in that portion of your interview. You know, in fact, this was a camp; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: You interrupted me when I spoke earlier on. I wanted to explain more extensively so that we could be understanding each other. At this moment, on the basis of the document that I first saw in 2003, it says the investigative centre. That's what it says in the letterhead. That's the document that I'm speaking of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Let's have 65 ter 33385, page 122.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now we see your answer in another part of your purportedly truthful OTP interview here at the bottom of the page. You're discussing Omarska. And you say in the second line: "I will now call it by its real name, camp Omarska." And in B/C/S you can see the words [B/C/S spoken], do you stand by that portion of your OTP interview as truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, where did we see the words "the true name." Oh, I see in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I believe it's the phrase that starts [B/C/S spoken], which I understand as "now I will."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And [B/C/S spoken] would then be the -- I don't see the translation yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's on the right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's now on the right. It wasn't before. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now you were asked about this camp in the Stakic case and I want to just show you part of that testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 33381, page 67.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's now P7625.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think it's been reserved for parts of it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you were asked: "From the moment when the facility the were taken over, could you in any way influence the developments at that site?" You responded: "Firstly, let me tell you that there was no way for me to do anything, to prevent these things. I'm afraid that at that -- that if I had received a document at that time, I would have made an attempt to prevent these things from happening. And I frankly don't know what would have happened to me." Now, first, do you stand by that part of your Stakic testimony?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What things that happened at camp Omarska did you mean that you would have attempted to prevent from happening?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: When I said to prevent, I would have prevented entry into the mine, if I could have. The establishment of the so-called investigative centre, on the basis of the original document. As for what happened inside the camp, I don't know what happened inside the camp, except for the books that I read written by people who had spent time there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now you heard at the time that people were being killed in Omarska; right? "At the time," meaning in 1992.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that it should be quoted in its entirety. It is true that I heard, listened, but then I did not believe these rumours because later on I encountered people who were still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, you discovered that not everyone in Omarska had been killed and consequently discounted what you had heard: That anyone who had been in Omarska had been killed?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what it is that you're trying to ask me. I'll try to answer. On the basis of all the rumours that were bandied about - I was not there, I don't know what happened there - later on it turned out that it was confirmed that people had been killed there. But I did not accept the initial rumours because people were saying in town, there were rumours that were being bandied about that certain people had been killed and then I saw those same people in town afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now you, yourself, could see dead bodies of killed Muslims and Croats in the town; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 33385, page 226.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we do that. Can I just ask: When later was it confirmed that people had been killed at Omarska? When did you get this confirmation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the war. After the exhumations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I, nevertheless, ask you a follow-up question. You say you saw people in town and therefore you didn't believe the rumours. Now, those persons, and perhaps you can name one of them, was it reported to you that they had been in Omarska and that, for that reason, you didn't believe the stories about persons being killed because you saw that person later; or was it reported to you that that person had been killed in Omarska and you didn't, therefore, believe the stories because you saw that person alive later. Which of the two? And perhaps you could just mention one example.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Generally speaking, concerning the killings that occurred in the territory of Prijedor, Pecani, a settlement that belongs to the town itself and Omarska and other areas belonging to Prijedor, there were stories that were being bandied about and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Listen. I'm only interested at this meant in relation to this question about Omarska. Could you give me one name that was -- that you saw later and ... because of seeing him you didn't believe the rumours about Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Softic, the optician.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was he reported to you as having been in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was told that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was told that he had come from Omarska, took all his equipment and moved to Split and that he gave money in order to be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was he reported as having been killed in Omarska to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, if rumours are that people are killed, why do you disbelieve those rumours because a person you knew who had been in Omarska but not having been reported to have been killed there, that you saw him alive? Why would that in any way contradict that others may have been killed there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can give you my assumption. They probably were. I was not there. I cannot say anything with certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's not an answer to my question. Although the beginning was. You said I don't know what to answer. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just one matter for the transcript. Sir, you were recorded to mention when you were discussing where you heard there been killings, you mentioned a place name Pecani, P-e-c-a-n-i. We see at line 20 of your OTP interview in response to the same question that you heard about killings in a place called Biscani, B-i-s-c-a-n-i, with diacritics in the appropriate places, of course. That's where you heard people had been killed; right.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You heard they were Muslims and Croats; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The entire settlement of Biscani are Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you heard there were hundreds of people killed there; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I didn't hear anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see we're at time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take the break. Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at 20 minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 31041.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you recognise the people in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Who's the man on the far right looking away from the camera?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
